Abstract

This research aimed to determine the optimal amount of Job’s Tears flour for producing the Thai dessert Thong Eak. The study investigated three basic recipes: Recipe 1 consisted of 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 10 grams of arrowroot flour, 230 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, 150 grams of egg yolk, and 5 grams of yellow food coloring. Recipe 2 consisted of 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 250 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, and 150 grams of egg yolk. Recipe 3 consisted of 90 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 220 grams of coconut milk, 170 grams of white granulated sugar, and 200 grams of egg yolk. These recipes were then evaluated for sensory quality using a 9-point hedonic scale with 50 panelists. Recipe 2 had the highest average overall acceptability score at 7.45, corresponding to a high level of liking, and was thus selected for product development by supplementing with Job’s Tears flour. Five levels of Job’s Tears flour were tested: 20% (20 grams), 40% (40 grams), 60% (60 grams), 80% (80 grams), and 100% (100 grams) respectively. When evaluated for sensory quality, statistically significant differences were found at the 95% confidence level (p < 0.05). The panelists most preferred the sample containing 80% Job’s Tears flour, with an average liking score in the "like very much" range. Subsequent physical quality analysis found L* (lightness), a* (redness), and b* (yellowness) values of 46.39, 13.81, and 37.29, respectively.

Introduction

Job’s Tears, also known by its common names Adlay, Adlay millet, or Job’s Tears (Coix lacryma-jobi L.), belongs to the grass family (POACEAE or GRAMINEAE) and the subfamily PANICOIDEAE. It is a type of cereal grain in the same family as rice. Job’s Tears is an annual plant with a monocotyledonous leaf. Its stem is soft-wooded, cylindrical, and upright, growing to a height of approximately 1-3 meters. It is native to Southeast Asia, and in Thailand, it is considered an economic crop commonly cultivated in the northern and northeastern regions. The plant has a distinctive aroma and is high in dietary fiber. The plant structure resembles that of corn, and its seeds are round to oval, white in color, with a slightly nutty taste. There are both edible and inedible varieties; the edible type has a softer fruit shell and is cultivated mainly for food purposes (Sunanta Thongtha, n.d.; Sunthorn Treenuntawan, 2010). Job’s Tears is a cereal grain with high nutritional value, rich in vitamins and minerals essential for the body. One hundred grams of Job’s Tears contains 372 kilocalories; 13.6 grams of protein, 3.7 grams of fat, 71.0 grams of carbohydrates, 3.4 grams of dietary fiber, 19 milligrams of calcium, 364 milligrams of phosphorus, 8.0 milligrams of iron, 0.38 milligrams of vitamin B1, 0.10 milligrams of vitamin B2, and 3.10 milligrams of vitamin B3 (Editorial Department, Sangdad Publishing, n.d.). Job’s Tears also contains a variety of amino acids, such as glutamic acid, leucine, alanine, proline, valine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, arginine, among others. In addition, Job’s Tears has numerous health benefits and properties that help nourish and promote bodily health in various ways. For example, it helps improve the digestive system and reduces constipation, as Job’s Tears is very high in dietary fiber, thereby aiding smooth bowel movements. It also promotes restful sleep because it contains amino acids that stimulate the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps induce sleep. Furthermore, the vitamin A present in Job’s Tears supports eye health, enhancing the ability to see in low light or at night. It also strengthens teeth and bones, helps prevent osteoporosis, nourishes tendons and joints, and contributes to radiant skin. Job’s Tears is rich in vitamins B1 and B2; regular consumption can help make the skin more beautiful and vibrant (Vichaiyut Hospital, 2020; Anonymous, 2020).

Khanom Thong Eak is a type of Thai dessert belonging to the “thong” (golden) family. It is presumed that this dessert did not originate in traditional Thai culture but instead was influenced by Indian or Middle Eastern Muslim cultures. The name “Thong Eak” carries an auspicious meaning, symbolizing wealth and prosperity. The ingredients of Khanom Thong Eak include flour mixed with egg yolk, sugar, and coconut milk. The preparation involves stirring the mixture until it forms a dough, which is then molded into beautiful shapes using intricately carved molds. After unmolding, the desserts are left to dry on the surface. Sometimes, they are scented with candle smoke for fragrance before being stored for eating. The finished dessert is fragrant, has a smooth and creamy sweet taste due to the sugar and coconut milk, and its color ranges from yellow to orange, varying from pale yellow or creamy yellow to deep orange, with small sheets of gold leaf attached for decoration, making it attractive. As such, Thong Eak is popularly given as a gift to bestow good fortune upon the recipient (Dinar Boontham & Waraporn Jiwchaisak, 2014).

However, it can be observed that the main ingredients used in Khanom Thong Eak are wheat flour, coconut milk, granulated sugar, and egg yolks from chicken or duck eggs. Consuming these in large amounts regularly can result in excessive intake of sugar, fat, and cholesterol—beyond the body's requirements—which may lead to various diseases (Sirimon Chaikate, Pornpen Morakotjinda, and Weena Thongrod, 2017), such as NCDs (Noncommunicable Diseases). NCDs are chronic non-communicable diseases that do not result from pathogens and cannot be transmitted from person to person but are caused by long-term unhealthy habits and behaviors, gradually leading to disease without being immediately apparent. NCDs include diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, central obesity, heart diseases, and vascular diseases, among others.

Therefore, this research sought to utilize flour made from Job’s Tears as an ingredient in the development of Thai dessert products, given its nutritional benefits and health value. Additionally, Job’s Tears is a locally cultivated plant in the northern and northeastern regions of Thailand, which helps promote the use of agricultural products among farmers. The aim is to create a Thai dessert that is nutritious and rich in various nutrients suitable for all genders and ages. Thus, Job’s Tears flour was developed as a key component in Thong Eak to supplement the standard recipe, studying the basic formula and appropriate quantity of Job’s Tears flour, in order to obtain a well-accepted Thong Eak product. This development could further expand into a commercially available product and serve as an alternative Thai dessert for health-conscious consumers in the future.

Study Methods/Research Methods  
1. Selection of the basic Thong Eak recipe

To study the basic recipe for Thong Eak, three different Thong Eak recipes (Table 1) were evaluated through sensory tests in various aspects, including appearance, color, aroma, taste, texture, softness and chewiness, and overall preference. The evaluation involved 50 panelists using a 9-point hedonic scale, where 9 points indicated the highest level of liking, followed by 8 points as the next most preferred (Pairoj Wiriyacharee, 2018). The experiment was designed as a Randomized Completely Block Design (RCBD). The results were assessed through statistical analysis, specifically Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) at a 95% confidence level, and differences were compared using Duncan’s New Multiple Range Test (DMRT) with statistical software.

Thong Eak production process:

1. Measure all ingredients and sift the all-purpose wheat flour, setting it aside.
2. Mix egg yolk with coconut milk thoroughly, then pour into the wheat flour and sugar mixture that has been prepared.
3. Gradually pour in and mix, stirring gently with a spatula until well combined.
4. Pour the entire mixture into a brass pan and place over low heat.
5. Stir gently with a spatula until the mixture separates from the pan, then remove from heat and let cool until it is just warm.
6. Compress the kneaded dough into molds, pressing gently without compacting too tightly, then unmold each piece.
7. Bake the Thong Eak in an oven at 50–60 degrees Celsius for 2 hours to remove moisture. The study of the optimal amount of Job’s Tears flour for producing Thong Eak began by developing the most accepted basic recipe identified in the initial phase. This base recipe was then used to create Job’s Tears flour-enriched Thong Eak by substituting Job’s Tears flour for all-purpose wheat flour at five levels: 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%, respectively. Subsequently, the physical quality of Thong Eak with varying amounts of Job’s Tears flour was analyzed for color parameters (L*, a*, and b*) using a colorimeter (HunterLab, Colorflex EZ 45-0 LAV model). Sensory evaluation was conducted covering appearance, color, aroma, taste, texture, chewiness, and overall preference by a panel of 50 testers using a 9-point hedonic scale, where 9 indicates the highest liking and 8 represents the next ranked preference (Pairoj Wiriyacharee, 2018). The experiment was designed using a Randomized Completely Block Design (RCBD) and analyzed statistically for variance (Analysis of Variance: ANOVA) at a 95% confidence level, with mean comparisons by Duncan’s New Multiple Range Test (DMRT) via statistical software.

Results and Discussion
Selection of the Basic Thong Eak Recipe
To select the optimal base recipe for future development of Job’s Tears flour-enriched Thong Eak, three basic recipes were tested and evaluated for sensory attributes (Table 2). Results showed that Recipe 2 was the most accepted by testers. There was no statistically significant difference (p>0.05) in terms of appearance. However, for color, aroma, taste, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, there were statistically significant differences among the recipes (p<0.05), with mean scores of 7.15, 7.30, 7.14, 7.28, 7.34, 7.42, and 7.45, respectively. Recipe 2 was consequently selected for further development with added Job’s Tears flour.

Results from the study on the optimal amount of Job’s Tears flour for producing Thong Eak using the selected basic recipe with five levels of substitution for all-purpose wheat flour (i.e., 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%; see Table 3) were then used for sensory evaluation. It was found that the 80% substitution level of Job’s Tears flour yielded the highest acceptance scores by testers. Appearance, color, aroma, taste, texture, chewiness, and overall preference exhibited statistically significant differences (p<0.05) with mean scores of 7.74, 7.28, 7.40, 7.85, 7.80, 7.90, and 7.92, respectively (Table 4). Increasing Job’s Tears flour content improved mold definition of the product when pressed but resulted in more noticeable cracks, lighter yellow color, and firmer, denser texture, which affected overall preference. At 100% Job’s Tears flour, the texture became relatively hard and coarse, causing lower scores in appearance smoothness, texture, and chewiness.

Summary of Experimental Results
From the study of basic recipes for Thong Eak, in which three different recipes were evaluated for sensory quality, it was found that testers most preferred Recipe 2. This recipe received the highest mean acceptance scores in visual appearance, color, aroma, flavor, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, with mean scores of 7.15, 7.30, 7.14, 7.28, 7.34, 7.42, and 7.45, respectively. The ingredients of Recipe 2 are as follows: 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 250 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, and 150 grams of egg yolk. Therefore, Recipe 2 was selected as the basic formula for developing Thong Eak supplemented with Job’s Tears flour, replacing the wheat flour at five levels: 20% (20 grams), 40% (40 grams), 60% (60 grams), 80% (80 grams), and 100% (100 grams), respectively. 

When these formulations were evaluated for sensory quality in terms of visual appearance, color, aroma, flavor, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, statistically significant differences were found (p<0.05). Testers most preferred the sample containing 80% Job’s Tears flour, which received mean scores of 7.74, 7.28, 7.40, 7.85, 7.80, 7.90, and 7.92, respectively. Physical quality analysis further revealed that the L*, a*, and b* color values of Thong Eak products supplemented with Job’s Tears flour ranged as follows: L* between 55.06–37.30, indicating a decrease in lightness; a* between 11.05–14.04, indicating a slight increase in redness; and b* between 44.79–34.77, showing a decrease in yellowness, respectively.

Abstract

This research aimed to determine the optimal amount of Job’s Tears flour for producing the Thai dessert Thong Eak. The study investigated three basic recipes: Recipe 1 consisted of 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 10 grams of arrowroot flour, 230 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, 150 grams of egg yolk, and 5 grams of yellow food coloring. Recipe 2 consisted of 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 250 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, and 150 grams of egg yolk. Recipe 3 consisted of 90 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 220 grams of coconut milk, 170 grams of white granulated sugar, and 200 grams of egg yolk. These recipes were then evaluated for sensory quality using a 9-point hedonic scale with 50 panelists. Recipe 2 had the highest average overall acceptability score at 7.45, corresponding to a high level of liking, and was thus selected for product development by supplementing with Job’s Tears flour. Five levels of Job’s Tears flour were tested: 20% (20 grams), 40% (40 grams), 60% (60 grams), 80% (80 grams), and 100% (100 grams) respectively. When evaluated for sensory quality, statistically significant differences were found at the 95% confidence level (p < 0.05). The panelists most preferred the sample containing 80% Job’s Tears flour, with an average liking score in the "like very much" range. Subsequent physical quality analysis found L* (lightness), a* (redness), and b* (yellowness) values of 46.39, 13.81, and 37.29, respectively.

Keywords: Thai dessert, Thong Eak, Job’s Tears flour, sensory evaluation

Introduction

Job’s Tears, also known by its common names Adlay, Adlay millet, or Job’s Tears (Coix lacryma-jobi L.), belongs to the grass family (POACEAE or GRAMINEAE) and the subfamily PANICOIDEAE. It is a type of cereal grain in the same family as rice. Job’s Tears is an annual plant with a monocotyledonous leaf. Its stem is soft-wooded, cylindrical, and upright, growing to a height of approximately 1-3 meters. It is native to Southeast Asia, and in Thailand, it is considered an economic crop commonly cultivated in the northern and northeastern regions. The plant has a distinctive aroma and is high in dietary fiber. The plant structure resembles that of corn, and its seeds are round to oval, white in color, with a slightly nutty taste. There are both edible and inedible varieties; the edible type has a softer fruit shell and is cultivated mainly for food purposes (Sunanta Thongtha, n.d.; Sunthorn Treenuntawan, 2010). Job’s Tears is a cereal grain with high nutritional value, rich in vitamins and minerals essential for the body. One hundred grams of Job’s Tears contains 372 kilocalories; 13.6 grams of protein, 3.7 grams of fat, 71.0 grams of carbohydrates, 3.4 grams of dietary fiber, 19 milligrams of calcium, 364 milligrams of phosphorus, 8.0 milligrams of iron, 0.38 milligrams of vitamin B1, 0.10 milligrams of vitamin B2, and 3.10 milligrams of vitamin B3 (Editorial Department, Sangdad Publishing, n.d.).

Job’s Tears also contains a variety of amino acids, such as glutamic acid, leucine, alanine, proline, valine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, arginine, among others. In addition, Job’s Tears has numerous health benefits and properties that help nourish and promote bodily health in various ways. For example, it helps improve the digestive system and reduces constipation, as Job’s Tears is very high in dietary fiber, thereby aiding smooth bowel movements. It also promotes restful sleep because it contains amino acids that stimulate the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps induce sleep. Furthermore, the vitamin A present in Job’s Tears supports eye health, enhancing the ability to see in low light or at night. It also strengthens teeth and bones, helps prevent osteoporosis, nourishes tendons and joints, and contributes to radiant skin. Job’s Tears is rich in vitamins B1 and B2; regular consumption can help make the skin more beautiful and vibrant (Vichaiyut Hospital, 2020; Anonymous, 2020).

Khanom Thong Eak is a type of Thai dessert belonging to the “thong” (golden) family. It is presumed that this dessert did not originate in traditional Thai culture but instead was influenced by Indian or Middle Eastern Muslim cultures. The name “Thong Eak” carries an auspicious meaning, symbolizing wealth and prosperity. The ingredients of Khanom Thong Eak include flour mixed with egg yolk, sugar, and coconut milk. The preparation involves stirring the mixture until it forms a dough, which is then molded into beautiful shapes using intricately carved molds. After unmolding, the desserts are left to dry on the surface. Sometimes, they are scented with candle smoke for fragrance before being stored for eating. The finished dessert is fragrant, has a smooth and creamy sweet taste due to the sugar and coconut milk, and its color ranges from yellow to orange, varying from pale yellow or creamy yellow to deep orange, with small sheets of gold leaf attached for decoration, making it attractive. As such, Thong Eak is popularly given as a gift to bestow good fortune upon the recipient (Dinar Boontham & Waraporn Jiwchaisak, 2014).

However, it can be observed that the main ingredients used in Khanom Thong Eak are wheat flour, coconut milk, granulated sugar, and egg yolks from chicken or duck eggs. Consuming these in large amounts regularly can result in excessive intake of sugar, fat, and cholesterol—beyond the body's requirements—which may lead to various diseases (Sirimon Chaikate, Pornpen Morakotjinda, and Weena Thongrod, 2017), such as NCDs (Noncommunicable Diseases). NCDs are chronic non-communicable diseases that do not result from pathogens and cannot be transmitted from person to person but are caused by long-term unhealthy habits and behaviors, gradually leading to disease without being immediately apparent. NCDs include diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, central obesity, heart diseases, and vascular diseases, among others.

Therefore, this research sought to utilize flour made from Job’s Tears as an ingredient in the development of Thai dessert products, given its nutritional benefits and health value. Additionally, Job’s Tears is a locally cultivated plant in the northern and northeastern regions of Thailand, which helps promote the use of agricultural products among farmers. The aim is to create a Thai dessert that is nutritious and rich in various nutrients suitable for all genders and ages. Thus, Job’s Tears flour was developed as a key component in Thong Eak to supplement the standard recipe, studying the basic formula and appropriate quantity of Job’s Tears flour, in order to obtain a well-accepted Thong Eak product. This development could further expand into a commercially available product and serve as an alternative Thai dessert for health-conscious consumers in the future.

Selection of the basic Thong Eak recipe

To study the basic recipe for Thong Eak, three different Thong Eak recipes (Table 1) were evaluated through sensory tests in various aspects, including appearance, color, aroma, taste, texture, softness and chewiness, and overall preference. The evaluation involved 50 panelists using a 9-point hedonic scale, where 9 points indicated the highest level of liking, followed by 8 points as the next most preferred (Pairoj Wiriyacharee, 2018). The experiment was designed as a Randomized Completely Block Design (RCBD). The results were assessed through statistical analysis, specifically Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) at a 95% confidence level, and differences were compared using Duncan’s New Multiple Range Test (DMRT) with statistical software.

Table 1 Basic recipes for Thong Eak

Ingredients (grams)        Recipe 1  Recipe 2  Recipe 3  
All-purpose wheat flour     100        100       90  
Arrowroot flour             10         -         -  
Coconut milk                230        250       220  
White granulated sugar      160        160       170  
Egg yolk (only yolk)        150        150       200  
Yellow food coloring        5          -         -  

Source: Recipe 1 – Areerat Noen Nam (2017); Recipe 2 – Srisomron Kongpun and Manee Suwanphong (1992); Recipe 3 – Phongsak Songpranam (2004)

Thong Eak production process:

1. Measure all ingredients and sift the all-purpose wheat flour, setting it aside.
2. Mix egg yolk with coconut milk thoroughly, then pour into the wheat flour and sugar mixture that has been prepared.
3. Gradually pour in and mix, stirring gently with a spatula until well combined.
4. Pour the entire mixture into a brass pan and place over low heat.
5. Stir gently with a spatula until the mixture separates from the pan, then remove from heat and let cool until it is just warm.

The study of the optimal amount of Job’s Tears flour for producing Thong Eak began by developing the most accepted basic recipe identified in the initial phase. This base recipe was then used to create Job’s Tears flour-enriched Thong Eak by substituting Job’s Tears flour for all-purpose wheat flour at five levels: 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%, respectively. Subsequently, the physical quality of Thong Eak with varying amounts of Job’s Tears flour was analyzed for color parameters (L*, a*, and b*) using a colorimeter (HunterLab, Colorflex EZ 45-0 LAV model). Sensory evaluation was conducted covering appearance, color, aroma, taste, texture, chewiness, and overall preference by a panel of 50 testers using a 9-point hedonic scale, where 9 indicates the highest liking and 8 represents the next ranked preference (Pairoj Wiriyacharee, 2018). The experiment was designed using a Randomized Completely Block Design (RCBD) and analyzed statistically for variance (Analysis of Variance: ANOVA) at a 95% confidence level, with mean comparisons by Duncan’s New Multiple Range Test (DMRT) via statistical software.

Results and Discussion
Selection of the Basic Thong Eak Recipe
To select the optimal base recipe for future development of Job’s Tears flour-enriched Thong Eak, three basic recipes were tested and evaluated for sensory attributes (Table 2). Results showed that Recipe 2 was the most accepted by testers. There was no statistically significant difference (p>0.05) in terms of appearance. However, for color, aroma, taste, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, there were statistically significant differences among the recipes (p<0.05), with mean scores of 7.15, 7.30, 7.14, 7.28, 7.34, 7.42, and 7.45, respectively. Recipe 2 was consequently selected for further development with added Job’s Tears flour.

Summary of Experimental Results
From the study of basic recipes for Thong Eak, in which three different recipes were evaluated for sensory quality, it was found that testers most preferred Recipe 2. This recipe received the highest mean acceptance scores in visual appearance, color, aroma, flavor, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, with mean scores of 7.15, 7.30, 7.14, 7.28, 7.34, 7.42, and 7.45, respectively. The ingredients of Recipe 2 are as follows: 100 grams of all-purpose wheat flour, 250 grams of coconut milk, 160 grams of white granulated sugar, and 150 grams of egg yolk. Therefore, Recipe 2 was selected as the basic formula for developing Thong Eak supplemented with Job’s Tears flour, replacing the wheat flour at five levels: 20% (20 grams), 40% (40 grams), 60% (60 grams), 80% (80 grams), and 100% (100 grams), respectively. 

When these formulations were evaluated for sensory quality in terms of visual appearance, color, aroma, flavor, texture, chewiness, and overall preference, statistically significant differences were found (p<0.05). Testers most preferred the sample containing 80% Job’s Tears flour, which received mean scores of 7.74, 7.28, 7.40, 7.85, 7.80, 7.90, and 7.92, respectively. Physical quality analysis further revealed that the L*, a*, and b* color values of Thong Eak products supplemented with Job’s Tears flour ranged as follows: L* between 55.06–37.30, indicating a decrease in lightness; a* between 11.05–14.04, indicating a slight increase in redness; and b* between 44.79–34.77, showing a decrease in yellowness, respectively.
